content: Glycine, often abbreviated as Gly or G, is an organic compound with the chemical formula NH2CH2COOH. It is the smallest of the 20 amino acids commonly found in proteins, as its side chain consists of only two hydrogen atoms. This simplicity makes glycine unique among proteinogenic amino acids, as it is not chiral. Due to its small size and lack of chirality, glycine can integrate into both hydrophilic and hydrophobic environments. Its codons are GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG. Glycine appears as a colorless, sweet-tasting crystalline solid. Production and Key Properties Glycine was first discovered in 1820 by Henri Braconnot, who obtained it by boiling gelatin with sulfuric acid. Industrially, glycine is synthesized by reacting chloroacetic acid with ammonia, producing approximately 15 million kilograms annually. In the United States, glycine is manufactured by GEO Specialty Chemicals, Inc., and Chattem Chemicals, Inc., while in Japan, it is produced by Shoadenko. GEO Specialty Chemicals employs a semi-batch process that results in glycine with residual sulfate but no chloride, whereas Chattem Chemicals uses a batch process (MCA process) that yields glycine with residual chloride but no sulfate. Glycine has two pKa values: 2.35 and 9.78. At a pH above 9.78, glycine predominantly exists as the anionic amine form (H2NCH2CO2-), while at a pH below 2.35, it exists as the cationic carboxylic acid form (H3N+CH2CO2H). Its isoelectric point (pI) is 6.06. Biosynthesis Glycine is not an essential amino acid for humans, as it can be synthesized in the body from serine, which itself is derived from 3-phosphoglycerate. The enzyme serine hydroxymethyltransferase, with the cofactor pyridoxal phosphate, catalyzes this conversion. In vertebrate livers, glycine can also be synthesized by glycine synthase (also known as the glycine cleavage enzyme), a reaction that is reversible. Glycine is encoded by the codons GGU, GGC, GGA, and GGG. While most proteins contain only small amounts of glycine, collagen is an exception, as it is composed of approximately 35% glycine. Degradation Glycine is degraded through three primary pathways. The predominant pathway in animals involves the glycine cleavage enzyme, which also plays a role in glycine biosynthesis. This degradation pathway is essentially the reverse of the synthetic process. In the second pathway, glycine is first converted back to serine by serine hydroxymethyltransferase. Serine is then degraded to pyruvate by serine dehydratase. In the third pathway, glycine is oxidized to glyoxylate by D-amino acid oxidase. Glyoxylate is subsequently converted to oxalate by hepatic lactate dehydrogenase in an NAD+-dependent reaction. Physiological Functions The primary role of glycine is as a precursor for protein synthesis. It also serves as a building block for various natural products. As a Biosynthetic Intermediate In higher eukaryotes, glycine is a precursor for the synthesis of D-aminolevulinic acid, a key intermediate in the biosynthesis of porphyrins. Additionally, glycine contributes the central C2N subunit in the synthesis of all purines. As a Neurotransmitter Glycine functions as an inhibitory neurotransmitter in the central nervous system, particularly in the spinal cord, brainstem, and retina. When glycine receptors are activated, chloride ions enter the neuron through ionotropic receptors, leading to an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP). Strychnine is a potent antagonist of ionotropic glycine receptors, while bicuculline is a weaker antagonist. Glycine also acts as a co-agonist with glutamate at NMDA receptors, which are excitatory. Unlike its inhibitory role in the spinal cord, glycine facilitates excitatory activity at NMDA glutaminergic receptors. The oral LD50 of glycine in rats is 7930 mg/kg, with death typically resulting from hyperexcitability. Commercial Uses In the United States, glycine is sold in two primary grades: United States Pharmacopeia (USP) grade and technical grade. USP-grade glycine accounts for 80–85% of the U.S. market and is used in pharmaceutical applications, such as intravenous injections, where high purity is required. Pharmaceutical-grade glycine is often manufactured to proprietary specifications and is sold at a premium compared to USP-grade glycine. Technical-grade glycine, which may or may not meet USP standards, is used in industrial applications, such as metal complexing and finishing, and is typically sold at a lower price. Animal and Human Foods USP-grade glycine is also used as an additive in pet food and animal feed. For human consumption, glycine is marketed as a sweetener and taste enhancer. It is also included in food supplements and protein drinks. Certain drug formulations incorporate glycine to improve gastric absorption. Cosmetics and Miscellaneous Applications Glycine is used as a buffering agent in antacids, analgesics, antiperspirants, cosmetics, and toiletries. It is also utilized in the production of rubber sponge products, fertilizers, and metal complexants. Chemical Feedstock Glycine serves as an intermediate in the synthesis of various chemical products, including the herbicide glyphosate. Glyphosate, chemically known as N-(phosphonomethyl)glycine, is a non-selective systemic herbicide used to eliminate weeds, particularly perennials. It is applied either broadly or in cut-stump treatments as a forestry herbicide. Initially, glyphosate was sold exclusively by Monsanto under the trade name Roundup, but it is no longer under patent. Presence in Space The presence of glycine in the interstellar medium has been a topic of debate. In 2008, the glycine-like molecule aminoacetonitrile was identified in the Large Molecule Heimat, a massive gas cloud near the galactic center in the constellation Sagittarius, by the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy. In 2009, glycine was confirmed in samples collected in 2004 from comet Wild 2 by NASA's Stardust spacecraft. This discovery marked the first confirmed detection of extraterrestrial glycine and provided support for the panspermia hypothesis, which posits that the building blocks of life are widespread throughout the universe.
